panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (Left, Middle, Right). Left: Left panel is a clinical photograph of the patient's oropharynx showing orange-yellow enlarged tonsils, a classic manifestation of Tangier disease described in the article. Middle: Middle panel is a clinical photograph of the patient's distended abdomen, consistent with the reported massive hepatosplenomegaly. No exact Tangier-disease finding key is in the provided vocabulary, so the visible manifestation is proposed. Right: Right panel shows the patient's hands with digital clubbing, mentioned in the physical examination in the setting of genetically confirmed Tangier disease. Clubbing is nonspecific and not a classic Tangier-disease manifestation; attribution is therefore low-confidence.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Colonoscopy image from patient #3 in a Tangier disease case series, showing the patient's gastrointestinal manifestation with edematous mucosa and hyperpigmentation. B: PAS-stained colonic biopsy from a Tangier disease patient, showing focal aggregation of macrophages with large foamy cytoplasm and granular PAS positivity, consistent with foam cell infiltration. C: CD68 immunohistochemistry of colonic biopsy from a Tangier disease patient, marking macrophage infiltration corresponding to the foam cell aggregates seen on PAS staining.

panels.figure_caption: Endoscopic images from colonoscopy of patient #3 showing edematous mucosa with hyperpigmentation (A) and histological images from the colonic biopsies showing focal aggregation of macrophages with large foamy cytoplasm and granular PAS positivity (arrows), both in the mucosa and submucosa: (B) PAS staining; (C) immunohistochemistry for CD68 marking macrophages (dark grey). Abbreviation: PAS, periodic acid-Schiff.
in_text_mentions: #3 presented with a pronounced gastrointestinal manifestation discovered on combined esophagoduodenoscopy with colonoscopy to rule out gastrointestinal malignancy. The most remarkable findings were hyperpigmentation and edematous thickening of the colonic mucosa in all segments as well as irregular duodenitis (Fig. 1A). Histological evaluation revealed pronounced focal infiltration of the mucosa and the submucosa by CD68-positive foam cells [Fig. 1B and 1C, Supplemental Fig. S1 (17)] and several polyps formed predominantly by foam cells with iron deposition [Supplementary Figs. S2 and 3 (17)].

A: Real patient colon biopsy histology (10×) from an ABCA1/Tangier disease family; caption and in-text state the biopsy showed foamy histiocytes, a recognized lipid-laden histiocyte manifestation of Tangier disease. The colon foam-cell finding is not represented by a vocabulary key (the foam-cell key is tonsil-specific), so it is placed in proposed_findings. B: Real patient colon biopsy histology (20×) from the Tangier disease (ABCA1) family case; foamy histiocytes are explicitly captioned and supported by in-text as a described TD finding. Colon foam-cell manifestation is absent from the vocabulary (foam-cell key is tonsil-specific), so it is proposed rather than force-mapped. C: Real patient colon biopsy histology (40×) from the Tangier disease (ABCA1) family; foamy histiocytes captioned and corroborated by in-text as previously described in TD. No colon-specific foam-cell vocabulary key exists (the foam-cell key is tonsil-specific), so...

A: Caption and in-text explicitly identify these as dorsal skin lesions of the patient with Tangier Disease described in the study; the article title confirms an atypical form of Tangier disease. The manifestation is not represented in the allowed findings vocabulary, so it is recorded as a proposed finding. [raw subtype: atypical_form] B: Caption identifies panel B as the same Tangier Disease patient's dorsal lesions after 6 months of miglustat treatment, showing improvement. It remains a real patient image of the target disease with residual visible dorsal findings, attributed by the caption and article title to Tangier disease. Skin biopsy of one dorsal nodular lesion was performed. During this period the patient showed a progressive amelioration of the skin lesions (Figure 3B) and a subjective improvement of general and mental wellbeing, with less fatigue and faster thought processes. No substantial improvements were noted in spleen volume, blood counts and plasma levels of HDL, ApoA1, total cholesterol and triglycerides.

Pictures taken A after 7 months of miglustat discontinuation; B after 6 months of miglustat treatment.

attribution_variants: Sechi et al. Effects of miglustat treatment in a patient affected by an atypical form of Tangier disease.. Orphanet journal of rare diseases 2014. doi:10.1186/s13023-014-0143-3. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
